question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2021, behavioral ecologist Teodora Pellanor claimed that ashcrest warblers in brightly lit city districts begin their dawn song earlier than rural ashcrest warblers do, because night lighting shifts the birds' internal daily clock earlier.
• A team led by Anselm Verrick at the Hadleigh Field Station recorded dawn song at 20 brightly lit city sites and 20 dark rural sites during one May.
• At the lit sites, the warblers began singing an average of 52 minutes before sunrise; at the dark sites, they began an average of 31 minutes before sunrise.
• The team also captured 24 warblers from lit districts and 24 from dark rural areas and housed each bird alone in an aviary kept in constant dim light with no changes in brightness during the day.
• The team recorded the time of day at which each bird's daily activity began, measured by perch movement sensors.
• Activity began at an average of 5:46 a.m. for the birds from lit districts and 5:46 a.m. for the birds from dark rural areas.
• Song recordings were made at each site on 10 mornings, using automated microphones mounted about 3 meters above the ground.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Pellanor's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings bear out Pellanor's observation but not her explanation: the warblers at lit sites began singing an average of 52 minutes before sunrise to the dark sites' 31 minutes, yet the two groups of aviary birds began their daily activity at the same average time, 5:46 a.m.
answer_b: The team's findings undermine Pellanor's claim: the birds from lit districts and the birds from dark rural areas began their daily activity at the same average time in the aviary, 5:46 a.m.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Pellanor's claim: the warblers at lit sites began singing an average of 52 minutes before sunrise, compared with an average of 31 minutes before sunrise at dark sites.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Pellanor's claim and show the two groups were otherwise comparable: the warblers at lit sites began singing an average of 52 minutes before sunrise to the dark sites' 31 minutes, and the aviary birds from both kinds of areas began their daily activity at the same average time, 5:46 a.m.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer because it matches each part of Pellanor's claim to the data that bears on it. Pellanor's sentence says two things: that warblers in brightly lit districts begin their dawn song earlier than rural warblers do, and that this happens because night lighting shifts the birds' internal daily clock earlier. The song recordings bear on the first part. At the lit sites the warblers began singing an average of 52 minutes before sunrise, compared with 31 minutes before sunrise at the dark sites, so the earlier dawn song Pellanor described did appear. The aviary measurement bears on the second part. In constant dim light with no changes in brightness, the time at which a bird's daily activity begins reflects its own internal clock rather than any light cue, so it shows whether the clocks of city birds are set earlier. The birds from lit districts and the birds from dark rural areas both began activity at an average of 5:46 a.m., so there was no sign of an earlier internal clock in the city birds. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about the number of recording mornings and the microphone placement describe the method and do not bear on either part.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The identical aviary activity times (5:46 a.m. for both groups) do count against Pellanor's explanation about the internal clock, but the claim also says that city warblers begin dawn song earlier, and the song recordings (52 versus 31 minutes before sunrise) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The 52 versus 31 minutes before sunrise do fit the first part of Pellanor's claim, that lit-district warblers sing earlier, but she also said this happens because night lighting shifts the internal clock earlier, and the aviary results (5:46 a.m. for both groups) show no such shift. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads the aviary result as a control rather than as a test of the explanation. The notes describe the aviary measurement as a record of when each bird's activity began with no time-of-day light cues, which is the internal clock Pellanor's 'because' clause is about. The identical times (5:46 a.m.) therefore show that the clocks of the two groups did not differ, which fails to support her explanation instead of confirming it. Nothing in the notes presents the measurement as a check that the groups were otherwise comparable. This is the pattern of reading a null result on the mechanism as added support for the claim.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2021, comparative psychologist Verrin Aldecott claimed that pet dogs follow a human's pointing gesture to hidden food more accurately than shelter dogs that have had little contact with people do, because pet dogs pay more attention to human faces.
• A team led by Odalys Pellwick at the Marrowfield Canine Cognition Laboratory tested 40 pet dogs and 40 shelter dogs that had had little contact with people.
• In a pointing task, each dog watched an experimenter point to the one of two overturned cups that concealed a food treat (the other cup was empty) and was then released to choose a cup; each dog completed 10 trials.
• The pet dogs chose the pointed-to cup in an average of 8.1 of the 10 trials; the shelter dogs did so in an average of 5.9.
• In a separate task, each dog sat facing a video screen on which an experimenter spoke in a friendly tone for two minutes while a camera tracked the dog's gaze.
• The pet dogs spent an average of 34 percent of the two minutes looking at the experimenter's eyes and mouth; the shelter dogs spent an average of 35 percent.
• All testing took place in a quiet room at the laboratory, with the dogs' handlers or caregivers waiting outside the room.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Aldecott's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings undermine Aldecott's claim: the pet dogs and the shelter dogs spent nearly the same share of the two minutes looking at the experimenter's eyes and mouth, 34 percent versus 35 percent.
answer_b: The team's findings bear out Aldecott's claim: the pet dogs chose the pointed-to cup in an average of 8.1 of the 10 trials, compared with an average of 5.9 for the shelter dogs.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out the observation in Aldecott's claim but not its explanation: the pet dogs chose the pointed-to cup in an average of 8.1 of the 10 trials to the shelter dogs' 5.9, yet the two groups spent nearly the same share of the two minutes looking at the experimenter's eyes and mouth, 34 percent versus 35 percent.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Aldecott's claim and strengthen it: the pet dogs chose the pointed-to cup in an average of 8.1 of the 10 trials to the shelter dogs' 5.9, and because the two groups spent nearly the same share of the two minutes looking at the experimenter's eyes and mouth, 34 percent versus 35 percent, the groups differed in little other than their contact with people.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it matches each part of Aldecott's claim to the data that bears on it. Aldecott's sentence says two things: that pet dogs follow a human's pointing gesture to hidden food more accurately than shelter dogs with little human contact, and that this happens because pet dogs pay more attention to human faces. The pointing task bears on the first part. The pet dogs chose the pointed-to cup in an average of 8.1 of 10 trials, compared with 5.9 for the shelter dogs, so the greater accuracy Aldecott described did appear. The video-screen task bears on the second part, because the share of the two minutes spent looking at the experimenter's eyes and mouth is a measure of how much attention a dog pays to a human face. There the pet dogs averaged 34 percent and the shelter dogs 35 percent, so the pet dogs showed no greater attention to the face. The team's findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about the testing room and the handlers' location describe the study's method and do not bear on either part.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The nearly equal shares of the two minutes spent looking at the experimenter's eyes and mouth (34 percent versus 35 percent) do count against Aldecott's explanation, but the claim also says that pet dogs follow a pointing gesture more accurately, and the pointing results (8.1 versus 5.9 trials) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The 8.1 versus 5.9 pointing averages do fit the first part of Aldecott's claim, that pet dogs follow a pointing gesture more accurately, but Aldecott also said this happens because pet dogs pay more attention to human faces, and the gaze results (34 percent versus 35 percent) show no such difference. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads the gaze result as a control rather than as a test of the explanation. The share of the two minutes spent looking at the experimenter's eyes and mouth is the very quantity Aldecott's explanation is about, so the near-identical values (34 percent versus 35 percent) show that pet dogs did not attend more to faces, which counts against Aldecott's explanation rather than strengthening the claim. The notes also give no basis for concluding that the groups differed only in contact with people. This is the pattern of treating a measure that fails the mechanism as evidence that the groups were otherwise comparable.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2024, sports scientist Ingrid Pellerin-Voss claimed that distance runners wearing the Strideline Arc, a shoe with a curved carbon plate in the sole, finish a fixed race distance faster than they do in standard shoes, because the plate reduces the energy their bodies must spend at any given pace.
• A team led by Desmond Thackeray-Lind at the Ravelstone Exercise Physiology Laboratory studied 24 trained distance runners, each of whom completed both parts of the study in both shoe types.
• In the first part, each runner completed two 5-kilometer time trials on an outdoor track, one week apart, wearing the Strideline Arc in one trial and a standard shoe in the other; the order was alternated across runners.
• The runners' mean time was 19 minutes 42 seconds in the Strideline Arc and 20 minutes 18 seconds in the standard shoe.
• In the second part, each runner ran on a treadmill at a fixed pace of 15 kilometers per hour for six minutes in each shoe type while a mask measured the oxygen the runner consumed.
• The runners' mean oxygen consumption was 48.2 milliliters per kilogram of body mass per minute in the Strideline Arc and 48.1 milliliters per kilogram per minute in the standard shoe.
• Both parts took place in the laboratory's indoor facility and adjacent track during a single spring month, with all runners wearing the same brand of socks.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Pellerin-Voss's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings undermine Pellerin-Voss's claim: the runners' mean oxygen consumption at the fixed pace was 48.2 milliliters per kilogram per minute in the Strideline Arc and 48.1 in the standard shoe.
answer_b: The team's findings bear out Pellerin-Voss's claim: the runners' mean 5-kilometer time was 19 minutes 42 seconds in the Strideline Arc, compared with 20 minutes 18 seconds in the standard shoe.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Pellerin-Voss's claim and show the runners were equally fit in both conditions: the mean 5-kilometer time was 19 minutes 42 seconds in the Strideline Arc versus 20 minutes 18 seconds in the standard shoe, and mean oxygen consumption was 48.2 milliliters per kilogram per minute versus 48.1.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Pellerin-Voss's observation but not her explanation: the runners' mean 5-kilometer time was 19 minutes 42 seconds in the Strideline Arc versus 20 minutes 18 seconds in the standard shoe, yet mean oxygen consumption at the fixed pace was 48.2 milliliters per kilogram per minute versus 48.1.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer because it matches each part of Pellerin-Voss's claim to the data that bears on it. Her sentence says two things: that runners in the Strideline Arc finish a fixed distance faster than they do in standard shoes, and that this happens because the plate reduces the energy their bodies must spend at any given pace. The time trials bear on the first part. The runners' mean 5-kilometer time was 19 minutes 42 seconds in the Strideline Arc and 20 minutes 18 seconds in the standard shoe, so the faster finish she described did appear. The treadmill measurement bears on the second part, because oxygen consumption at a fixed pace is a direct measure of how much energy the body is spending at that pace. There the mean was 48.2 milliliters per kilogram per minute in the Strideline Arc and 48.1 in the standard shoe, so the plated shoe did not lower the energy the runners spent. The team's findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about the number of runners, the month of testing, and the socks describe the study's method and do not bear on either part.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The nearly identical oxygen consumption figures (48.2 versus 48.1) do count against Pellerin-Voss's explanation, but her claim also says that runners finish a fixed distance faster in the Strideline Arc, and the time trials (19 minutes 42 seconds versus 20 minutes 18 seconds) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The faster mean time in the Strideline Arc does fit the first part of Pellerin-Voss's claim, but she also said this happens because the plate reduces the energy the body spends at a given pace, and the oxygen consumption figures (48.2 versus 48.1 milliliters per kilogram per minute) show no such reduction. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it misreads the oxygen consumption result as a control rather than as a test of the explanation. Each runner completed both conditions, and the notes say nothing about the runners' fitness differing, so the nearly identical figures (48.2 versus 48.1) do not show equal fitness. They show that the plated shoe did not lower the energy spent at a fixed pace, which fails to support the 'because' clause of the claim. This is the pattern of reading a null result on the mechanism measure as added confirmation of the whole claim.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2021, cognitive aging researcher Wynne Tasburgh claimed that adults aged 65 to 80 who play the strategy board game Hexamar weekly recall grocery lists better than adults who do not play it, because the game trains the ability to hold and rearrange several pieces of information in mind at once.
• A team led by Piet Sundqvist at the Ketterly Institute on Aging tested 60 adults aged 65 to 80 who had played Hexamar at least once a week for three years and 60 adults of the same ages who had never played it.
• In a recall task, each participant heard a list of 15 common grocery items read aloud once, spent 10 minutes on unrelated puzzles, and then wrote down as many of the items as possible.
• The Hexamar players recalled an average of 10.4 of the 15 items; the non-players recalled an average of 7.8.
• In a separate task, each participant heard strings of digits read aloud at a rate of one digit per second and then repeated each string in reverse order, beginning with strings of three digits and adding one digit at a time until two consecutive errors occurred.
• The longest string repeated correctly in reverse averaged 5.0 digits for the Hexamar players and 5.1 digits for the non-players.
• Each participant was tested individually at a community center near home, in a single session of about 40 minutes.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Tasburgh's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings undermine Tasburgh's claim: the longest string repeated correctly in reverse averaged 5.0 digits for the Hexamar players and 5.1 digits for the non-players, a difference too small to indicate any advantage for the players.
answer_b: The team's findings bear out Tasburgh's observation but not her explanation: the Hexamar players recalled an average of 10.4 of the 15 items to the non-players' 7.8, yet the longest string repeated correctly in reverse averaged 5.0 digits for the players and 5.1 for the non-players.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Tasburgh's claim: the Hexamar players recalled an average of 10.4 of the 15 grocery items, compared with an average of 7.8 for the non-players, a gap that fits her description of the players' advantage.
answer_d: The team's findings strengthen Tasburgh's claim: the Hexamar players recalled an average of 10.4 of the 15 items to the non-players' 7.8, and because the longest reversed strings were nearly identical, 5.0 digits versus 5.1, the recall advantage cannot be attributed to a general difference between the groups.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it matches each part of Tasburgh's claim to the data that bears on it. Tasburgh's sentence says two things: that adults aged 65 to 80 who play Hexamar weekly recall grocery lists better than non-players, and that this happens because the game trains the ability to hold and rearrange several pieces of information in mind at once. The recall task bears on the first part. The players recalled an average of 10.4 of the 15 items, compared with 7.8 for the non-players, so the recall advantage Tasburgh described did appear. The reverse-order digit task bears on the second part. To repeat a heard string of digits backward, a person has to keep the digits available and reorder them before answering, so the longest string repeated correctly in reverse indicates how well a person can do what Tasburgh says the game trains. The players' average of 5.0 digits was no higher than the non-players' average of 5.1, so the players showed no stronger ability of this kind. The team's findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about the number of participants, their ages, and the testing setting describe the study's method and do not bear on either part.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The nearly equal reverse-order digit results (5.0 versus 5.1) do count against Tasburgh's explanation, but the claim also says that Hexamar players recall grocery lists better, and the recall results (10.4 versus 7.8 items) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The 10.4 versus 7.8 recall averages do fit the first part of Tasburgh's claim, but she also said the advantage exists because the game trains the ability to hold and rearrange several pieces of information, and the reverse-order digit results (5.0 versus 5.1) show no such advantage for the players. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads the digit task as a check on whether the groups were alike rather than as a test of Tasburgh's explanation. The nearly identical digit results (5.0 versus 5.1) bear on the claim that the game trains the ability to hold and rearrange information, and they show the players did not have that ability to a greater degree, which weakens the explanation rather than strengthening it. The notes also give no basis for concluding that the groups were matched on general ability. This is the pattern of recasting a measure that fails the mechanism as supportive background evidence.
